Systems in context

From point movement to returned indication

Follow two operating rods, two blade detector rods and positive locking in a four-rod point-machine study.

Four rods, four connections

Choose Guided tours → Follow a point machine. Each blade has its own operating rod and its own detector rod. The near blade is the one closest to the machine. The short connections reach it; the long connections pass beneath the near stock rail to the far blade. Operating rods transmit force; detector rods follow blade position. Two detector rods cover two different blades, rather than duplicating the same input.

Alstom · voestalpine Railway Systems

One arrangement among several

Alstom’s December 2015 P80 brochure describes two independent operating rods and two detection rods, with locking of both open and closed blades. The study uses that four-rod arrangement; its actuator, lock openings and contacts are functional illustrations. Other families differ: voestalpine UNISTAR HR separates power from drive/locking/detection modules and supports installations with or without stretcher bars; Vossloh MCEM91 uses internal locking; Siemens offers internal and external locking families. A stretcher bar couples blades; it is a different component from a detector rod or a separate lock rod.

Alstom · voestalpine Railway Systems · Vossloh · Siemens Mobility

Read A, neither and B

At A, the near blade is open and the far blade closed. The locks withdraw before the blades move, and neither end is indicated during travel. At B, the near blade is closed against its stock rail and the far blade is open for flange clearance. B is indicated only when both blade conditions and the locks are established. Use the stage buttons to inspect movement, locking and indication separately. The final step follows the returned indication to the interlocking.

Alstom · voestalpine Railway Systems

Compare missing conditions

In Stopped short, neither blade reaches its end position and the locks stay released. In One detector missing, both blades reach B and both locks engage. The far-blade input is unavailable, so B is still not indicated. Choose Follow the indication to see how the interlocking checks the point condition alongside train detection and conflicting-route checks.

From the control-room console to a railway observation

Inspect the control room, workplace equipment and technical-room dependencies.

Start with what occupies the room

A control centre contains consoles, displays, input devices, voice terminals, cables and supporting technical equipment. A host computer runs software applications; the applications provide the information and functions that operators use.

Health and Safety Executive · California High-Speed Rail Authority

Follow the installed workplace connections

A local computer sits near its keyboard and displays. A keyboard, video and mouse (KVM) interface can instead connect those peripherals to a computer in another room. One workstation can access several applications, and one application can run across several hosts.

G&D / Panoptec Europe · Barco · California High-Speed Rail Authority

Give communications SCADA its own scope

SCADA is not limited to traction power. The Metrolinx LRT design criteria include communications-equipment monitoring. Racomm publishes telecom SCADA acquisition from devices or native managers across several communications systems. PA audio, CCTV video and radio calls remain service payloads distinct from equipment-health points.

Metrolinx · Racomm

Name the point before drawing a connection

For each reported point, identify the equipment, the observed condition and the system that supplies it. Telecom SCADA can monitor conditions or carry specifically configured requests. A shared human–machine interface (HMI) brings selected services to one screen; those services retain their own control permissions.

Racomm · Siemens Mobility · Zenitel · Davicom

Keep requests, outcomes and service performance separate

A received request is not an accepted request; an accepted request is not a completed change. Fresh returned equipment information is separate again from the performance of its service. A responding camera does not prove an appropriate view or recording; a healthy amplifier does not prove station-wide audibility. Interfaces compares unavailable feedback and refused requests without operating equipment.

Health and Safety Executive · Racomm · Zenitel · Davicom

Continue into the human work

Equipment and application views supply context for the separate People & processes studies. Alarm acknowledgement, incident coordination, resolution and duty handover are human activities with their own responsibilities and evidence. A stored record alone does not establish a repaired condition.

What happens during a maintenance visit?

Follow the relationship between vehicle condition, yard allocation, technical work, test evidence and the handover back to operations.

A visit begins with a reason for work

A maintenance visit may follow a scheduled interval, a reported fault or measurements collected in service. The reason for the work determines the required road, equipment, parts and time. Some tasks can be completed beside the vehicle; others require a component to be removed and sent to a workshop. Start with the whole depot to locate reception, inspection, maintenance, washing and stabling, then follow the areas needed for the task.

Location and readiness are different information

Yard coordination connects vehicle identity, location, available destinations and assigned work. A train may wait in stabling for attention or occupy a maintenance road while work continues. Its location alone does not establish readiness for service. The Work handover view changes the destination, point arrangement and vehicle position, while a separate work boundary shows where protection is needed. The handover identifies the work and responsibility; signalling and work protection establish their own conditions.

Inspection produces evidence; diagnosis interprets it

Roll-by sensors measure selected features as the train passes, such as wheel shape or visible vehicle equipment. Stationary examination adds close inspection, gauges and diagnostic reports. These observations help locate a problem: a symptom may originate in a sensor, wire, controller, actuator or mechanical part. Compare the moving train and fixed portal with the stationary train and diagnostic connection. Both feed evidence into the maintenance decision.

Running-gear work changes both access and support

An inspection pit gives access below a vehicle while its wheels remain on the rails. Lifting jacks raise the body above the bogies; a bogie drop lowers a detached bogie while the body stays supported. Wheelsets can be measured and inspected for defects. Reprofiling can take place under the vehicle or after removal, depending on the equipment and work required. Reprofiling cuts material from the wheel to restore its running shape. Non-destructive inspection examines material condition without cutting the component apart. In Component maintenance, a brake bench shows how the caliper brings the pads against a stationary test disc.

Doors, climate equipment and traction need their own work

A door combines leaves, guides, a drive, locking and position sensing. Heating, ventilation and air-conditioning equipment combines airflow, heat exchange, refrigeration and controls. Traction equipment includes motors, mechanical drives and power electronics. Each needs checks suited to its function. Open the component covers to compare their parts, then use Sequence position to follow movement or diagnostic information. The converter bench is relevant to both rotary and linear-motor propulsion.

A completed repair needs the appropriate evidence

Component fixtures, stationary vehicle checks and a test road make different responses observable. Required checks follow the work performed and the applicable maintenance instructions. The result needs the equipment identity, test conditions and maintenance context to be useful. Demonstrating one repaired function is one part of maintenance release; commissioning a new or modified vehicle has a wider scope.

The handover connects work with operation

ORR distinguishes maintenance delivery and its release documentation from fleet-maintenance management’s return-to-operation role. The handover brings together the completed work, supporting checks and any remaining restrictions. Fleet allocation then connects the vehicle with an operational requirement, while railway control deals with its movement. Follow the links between the test fixture, work record, planning desk and departure road to see those responsibilities.

Follow the complete electrification chain

Trace power from the substation to the train and back, then compare where the four supply arrangements differ.

Compare collection and return

Start with Fourth rail · DC, then select Third rail · DC. Both collect power through a shoe touching a conductor rail. Fourth rail has a separate conductor and shoe for the normal return current. Third rail returns through wheel connections and the running rails. The side-by-side conductors in this teaching model make the two electrical paths visible.

Network Rail · Railway Engineering Institution (formerly PWI) · Siemens Mobility

A pantograph can collect AC or DC

Compare Overhead · DC with Overhead · AC. Both use a pantograph touching the contact wire and a return through the running rails. In the DC example, the substation rectifies AC into DC. In the conventional AC example, the train carries a transformer and line converter before the DC link and motor inverter.

Siemens Mobility · Siemens Mobility · ABB · Siemens Mobility

Follow the transformer’s two circuits

The pantograph connects to the transformer’s primary winding; wheelsets and running rails complete that supply circuit. Magnetic coupling transfers energy to the separate secondary winding, which feeds the line converter. The line converter converts the secondary AC to DC for the DC link. Amber traces the incoming supply and cyan marks its return. Copper traces the separate transformer secondary circuit. Open the converter enclosure to find the DC-link capacitor bank and motor inverter. The inverter feeds either the rotary motor or linear induction motor (LIM), according to your propulsion choice.

ABB · Indian Railways — CAMTECH · Siemens Mobility · Railway Technical Research Institute

Move between the chain and its equipment

Use the complete chain to locate each electrical function, then open the substation, guideway, vehicle or equipment close-up. The selected supply arrangement follows you between those views. Collection, power conversion and propulsion are separate choices, so changing a pantograph to a shoe keeps the selected motor. The circuits show connections; the static traces do not show the alternating direction or waveform of AC current.

Compare wheel rotation with vehicle travel

Adhesion is the grip at the wheel–rail contact. It links wheel torque to the force that moves or slows the vehicle.

Start with rolling, spin and slide

Watch the rim marker and the wheel centre against the fixed stripes. During rolling, rotation follows the distance travelled. During spin, the wheel turns too much for that distance; during slide, it turns too little. The centre follows the same path in these comparisons so the difference is easy to see. The animation illustrates the relationship rather than calculating a stopping distance. It shows rotary traction and friction braking; LIM traction develops thrust through a separate reaction rail.

RSSB · Railway Technical Research Institute

Compare brake control with sanding

Wheel-slide protection monitors wheel behaviour and changes applied braking effort. In Slide protection, the brake actuator and effort bar vary while the wheel turns. Sanding acts at a different place: the hopper, hose and nozzle deliver sand ahead of the wheel–rail contact to improve grip. Follow both mechanisms and compare their physical paths.

RSSB · Knorr-Bremse · Knorr-Bremse

Separate a measurement from the motion it describes

An axle sensor measures rotation. Spin or slide can make a speed estimate based on that measurement differ from the vehicle’s actual speed. The separate travel marker makes that difference visible. Follow the connected localization concepts to see how motion evidence is combined, or open the depot wheelset study to examine the component itself.

Find what a service needs to keep working

A second communication path helps with a lost connection, but the service still needs its other dependencies.

Trace one service at a time

Start with the station-information application. It has paths A and B. The power-supervision application has only path A in this example, and both applications share a power supply. Select Path A lost: station information retains path B while power supervision loses its connection. Then select Shared power lost to see both applications lose their required supply.

NIST · ENISA

Separate access, live data and recording

Identity unavailable removes the connection needed for a new operator request while keeping field indications available. Recorder unavailable breaks the recording branch while live information remains connected. These selected conditions help distinguish the services. A security zone groups assets with related security needs; a conduit is a communication connection between zones.

NIST · ENISA

Check the recovered state

Compare Restored, unchecked with Evidence checked. The connection returns first, while a configuration mismatch and recording gap remain. The later comparison adds checks of configuration and recording. Restoring recording can capture new events, but does not recreate the missed history. Open Configuration & change to follow how the observed state is compared with its records and supporting evidence.

Follow access through the whole journey

Connect physical passage, usable information, assistance and the boarding interface from street to train.

Read the connected route

Follow the entrance through the wide fare gate and near lift to the platform. Tactile surfaces, a display and an audible-information point support the journey. Violet communication links connect information and assistance; the teal line marks the selected step-free route. The example illustrates those connections with schematic dimensions.

European Union Agency for Railways

Find another route when a lift is unavailable

Lift unavailable stops the highlighted route before the near lift and displays a service message and assistance connection. The stairs remain a separate route. Alternate lift follows a different approach to the second lift while retaining the first lift’s outage marker. The passenger needs both a usable route and information that helps them find it.

TransLink

Continue through the train doorway

Boarding aid needed reaches the platform but stops at the gap beside the train. Aid in place adds a bridging plate and extends the path into the doorway. Reaching the platform and boarding the train are separate parts of the journey. Ticketing, information, station design, assistance and disruption can each affect whether the complete trip is usable.

Match a changed item with its evidence

Follow the agreed reference, the observed configuration, applicable evidence and the information passed to the receiving team.

Identify the item and the reference

Configuration includes hardware, software, settings and documents. A baseline is an agreed configuration used as the reference for controlled change; the installed item and its as-built record show what was actually fitted. The Configuration & change map keeps proposed, recorded and observed states separate. Select a stage to see the people, inputs, actions and outputs involved.

NIST · INCOSE

Check what the evidence covers

The verification stage connects the identified configuration with a question, results and exceptions. Ask whether the evidence applies to that item, its interfaces and its intended use. A report for version A may apply to B where that link is established; changing the report’s label cannot supply missing coverage. Follow the return arrow when a configuration or evidence mismatch needs more work.

IRSE Australasian Section · Crossrail Learning Legacy

Carry conditions into the next handover

Reconciliation brings the actual configuration, its records and the applicable evidence into agreement. It also records remaining issues and conditions. The receiving team needs that information for its decision. Asset handover, maintenance release, worksite handback and a duty handover concern different recipients and responsibilities, so each has a separate process map.

Read a station from boarding edge to equipment room

Explore the station’s spaces, then follow door movement, sensing and the information returned to control equipment.

Choose the physical edge

Compare the open platform with half-height and full-height barriers. A barrier separates the passenger area from the trainway; its doors provide openings for boarding. Trainway sensing is another layer, with LiDAR or paired radar as alternatives in this model. Changing to an end-access lesson keeps the selected boarding edge.

Federal Transit Administration / Transportation Technology Center / Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority · Siemens Mobility · ST Engineering

Follow movement before reading status

Play the boarding sequence. The platform-facing train doors move while those on the opposite side remain closed. With a barrier fitted, follow its drive and leaves. Pause after closing: the closed contact is made, but the lock bolt has not engaged yet. Continue to see the bolt engage and the returned locking indication update. Command, physical movement and reported condition are separate steps.

Nippon Signal · Portalp Railway · National Capital Region Transport Corporation

Locate the sensing area

The trainway, the space between the train and barrier, a door’s closing edge and the end-gate opening are different areas. The interspace lesson requires a fitted barrier. The gate lesson shows a separate hinge, latch and position contact. After an object or open gate is reported, its physical state remains visible. The associated camera provides another view for assessment.

Siemens Mobility · Portalp Railway · Wabtec · Molinari Sensors

Connect the passenger levels

Follow the stairs and lift between the platform and concourse. The lift car carries its own doors, while landing doors stay with the building. During the trip, the doors close, the cabin travels, and the doors beside the upper landing open. On the concourse, inspect the equipment room and follow its services to displays, help points and other passenger devices.

Handovers and the boundaries between teams

Learn which subject, evidence and responsibility is changing before drawing a process.

Start with the subject

Ask what needs to pass between teams or be coordinated across them. A changed component needs an updated configuration record. A completed asset needs a receiving team. Infrastructure work needs handback to operational control. Maintenance needs release information, and a new duty holder needs the current operating picture. Incident coordination connects continuing reports and actions. Six of the eight maps follow these examples. The other two connect infrastructure observations to follow-up evidence and distinguish physical work protection from displayed status.

Australian Rail Track Corporation · Frequentis

Configuration and change

Configuration management keeps the system and its records in agreement. A baseline identifies an agreed version; controlled change records how that version changes. For example, replacing a module with one that has a different connector can affect the interface definition, installation record and test scope. The decision to approve the change comes before implementation. Verification then checks the item actually installed, including any differences from the plan.

INCOSE · IRSE Australasian Section

Asset handover is a lifecycle interface

The receiving team needs more than a finished physical asset. It needs the configuration, test results, operating and maintenance information, support arrangements and a record of outstanding work. ARTC connects these readiness needs with commissioning and handover. Metrolinx distinguishes in-service information, handover records and asset-register updates. Follow the map to see how the recipients identify what they are accepting and how they will maintain its records.

Australian Rail Track Corporation · Metrolinx

Worksite handback concerns a different boundary

Worksite handback connects the actual condition after work with operational control. The work team describes what was completed, what remains and any restrictions. Other disciplines check dependent interfaces: finishing one task may leave another system awaiting work or information. The receiving controller needs to understand the resulting conditions. Handback information, electrical restoration and permission for a train movement have separate responsibilities.

Sydney Trains / Transport for NSW RailSafe · Australian Rail Industry Standards Organisation

Maintenance delivery, fleet readiness and duty continuity

ORR’s maintenance model separates the technical work and release documentation from fleet-maintenance management’s return-to-operation decision. The latter considers the vehicle’s intended use and any restrictions. Duty handover transfers a different subject: the current situation between people. HSE describes preparation, a two-way exchange and cross-checking by the incoming person. In both cases, unresolved issues need an identified owner and a route for follow-up.

Office of Rail and Road · Health and Safety Executive

Coordination continues while evidence develops

Incident coordination brings reports and responsible teams together. Operational assessment, passenger support and technical investigation can run in parallel, with each team returning updates to a shared record. Acknowledging an event records attention; resolving it requires evidence about the condition. Follow a component link from the map, then return to see who uses its information and what decision that information supports.

Frequentis · Health and Safety Executive

People, automation and train-control families

Understand what GoA changes without confusing a supplier, a radio or a staffing model with an operating function.

Begin with responsibilities

The role cards describe functions that railways allocate to people. One person may carry several functions, or several teams may share them. Traffic coordination, signalling control, power supervision, passenger support and maintenance use different information and produce different outputs. Read each card’s inputs, responsibilities and outputs together. A service plan describes intended operation; a movement authority gives permission for a defined train movement.

IRSE Netherlands · Siemens Mobility · Office of Rail and Road

GoA describes train-operating allocation

Grades of automation describe who performs train-operating tasks. In GoA1, the driver controls the train within the applicable protection arrangements. GoA2 automates driving with a driver present. GoA3 uses driverless operation with an onboard operating attendant. GoA4 supports routine operation without either role. These grades describe operating responsibilities, independently of the signalling supplier. Degraded operation and recovery still need defined arrangements.

ERTMS Users Group · Office of Rail and Road

Passenger and field responsibilities remain visible

Automated driving still requires passenger communication, assistance, emergency response, maintenance and control-room coordination. ORR’s GoA4 guidance addresses these responsibilities. The Community of Metros research summary records operators choosing to carry attendants for customer service even where the trains could operate unattended. The chosen staffing model therefore depends on passenger needs and operating conditions as well as technical capability.

Office of Rail and Road · Community of Metros / Imperial College Railway and Transport Strategy Centre

Keep families, functions and suppliers separate

The train-control map introduces conventional signalling, communications-based train control (CBTC) and the European Train Control System (ETCS). Protection, automatic operation, supervision, route control and detection are functions within these arrangements. Automatic train control (ATC) is a broad term whose use varies between sources. ETCS is part of the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS); automatic train operation (ATO) can be added as a separate function. SelTrac, Trainguard MT and Urbalis are supplier product families with their own architectures. Historical SelTrac sources may name Thales; Hitachi Rail acquired that business in May 2024.

Prover · ERTMS Users Group · European Commission, Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport · European Commission, Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport · Alstom · Siemens Mobility · Hitachi Rail

A device can belong in several explanations

A track circuit or axle counter detects the condition of a track section. A balise or other reference transponder supplies information when a train passes. A radio transports messages. These devices can support different control architectures. Start with a family overview, inspect the device, then return to the functional diagram to see how that system uses its information.

Read a communications system from endpoint to endpoint

Begin with a person or a physical condition, locate the equipment, and distinguish the information from the action it may support.

Start with a service and its locations

A communications drawing is easier to read when you start with its endpoints. A passenger using a help point, a position contact in a plant room, a crew member using a cab radio and a camera producing video are different sources. Their recipients differ too: an answering operator, a supervisory application, a fixed radio terminal or a video recorder. Follow one service through the focused studies. The locations—train, trackside equipment, station and central facilities—help you place its equipment within the railway.

Moxa · Transport for NSW · Network Rail · Zenitel

Separate passive connections, active equipment and supply

Installed fibre ends at a passive patch panel. A patch lead connects it to an optical transceiver in a powered switch. A router connects network scopes, while a separate power supply or UPS supports the electronics. Open and separate the equipment to see these parts; use Connections to follow the information they carry. In the onboard alternative, local devices connect within a consist, a group of vehicles treated as one network unit. A train backbone connects those consists.

Westermo · Westermo · Moxa · ABB

Read SCADA in both directions

Supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) collects information from equipment and can send permitted requests. In the status example, follow the damper position through its contact, input module, local controller and operator display. The command example adds a separate output path. Request, relay operation, physical movement and returned indication are different events. The animation slows their sequence down so you can compare them. In Stale indication, the display retains an old value after its link is lost, while the field equipment has a different position. Read the value together with its age and quality.

Transport for NSW · Siemens · Siemens Mobility · Health and Safety Executive

Keep voice and passenger outputs purposeful

A help point combines a button, microphone, loudspeaker and call electronics. Its assigned answering service receives the request, answers it and establishes a conversation. Operational radio uses a different access path: cab equipment and an antenna connect through radio infrastructure to a fixed terminal. Passenger information follows another chain, from content source through a local player to a screen. Public address (PA) adds an amplifier that supplies electrical power to loudspeakers. The enlarged cone movement shows how the driver works; speaker placement and room acoustics determine the listening result.

Zenitel · Network Rail · Televic Rail · Bosch Building Technologies · Zenitel

Distinguish observation from control and proof

A camera captures an image, a network carries its video, a recorder stores it and a viewing client displays it. An available live image does not establish that a recording exists. Access control separates a decision from a physical condition: the relay releases the lock while the door can remain closed; the contact changes when the leaf leaves its closed position. That contact then supplies the displayed door state. At each step, ask what was observed, which device supplied the information and what the receiving application can conclude from it.

Axis Communications · Axis Communications · Axis Communications

Follow both wheels through a turnout

Connect the point-machine setting to the switch, closure rails and fixed crossing.

Set the route before passage

Open Guided tours → Follow wheels through a turnout. A selects the straight route: near blade open, far blade closed. B selects the diverging route: near blade closed, far blade open. These are the same settings as in the point-machine study. The blades remain locked while the wheelset passes. Changing route returns the wheelset to its approach.

Bane NOR · Alstom

Follow the pair of rails

The closed blade and its stock rail establish the selected entry path. Closure rails connect the switch to the crossing. Follow both wheels on the same axle: on the straight route the far wheel passes the crossing, while on the diverging route the near wheel does. The other wheel runs beside that route’s check rail.

Bane NOR · Vossloh · voestalpine Railway Systems / Nortrak-Damy

Separate support from guidance

In Crossing close-up, look first at the wheel passing this fixed, tread-bearing crossing. Its tread receives support from the wing rail and crossing nose, and their contact regions can overlap. The flangeway lets the wheel’s flange pass. Where the intersecting flangeway breaks the running surface, support transfers between the wing rail and crossing nose as the wheel passes. Now look across the axle: the opposite check rail can guide the back of the other wheel’s flange, keeping the crossing wheel on the intended side of the nose.

Bane NOR · voestalpine Railway Systems · voestalpine Railway Systems Nortrak · RISSB

Recognise different crossing families

This study has a fixed common crossing. Bane NOR and Vossloh also describe movable crossings. In voestalpine’s movable-point example the nose is set against a wing rail to provide a continuous running edge; it has separate setting and locking needs. That is a different mechanism from the fixed crossing shown here. Some fixed frogs are self-guarded: raised casting features provide the guidance instead of separate opposite check rails. A fixed diamond has two common and two obtuse crossings; its separate view marks their layout without animating wheel contact. A crossover uses two turnouts.

Bane NOR · Vossloh · voestalpine Railway Systems · Rail Accident Investigation Branch

Rail spacing and curves are simplified so the parts remain visible. The wheelset follows the selected route; its rotation illustrates travel rather than calculating wheel–rail contact forces. Point indication is one of several conditions checked by the interlocking.

People, work and evidence

These maps organize responsibilities and evidence. They are conceptual studies, not operational instructions or a universal sequence of work.

Configuration & change

Keep the physical or software change, its interfaces and its evidence aligned.

  • Identify the affected baseline — Configuration / change coordinator
  • Examine consequences and evidence needs — Configuration / change coordinator
  • Record the change disposition — Asset recipient / responsible team
  • Relate implementation to the agreed subject — Maintenance / work-delivery lead
  • Examine the matching evidence — Test / verification team
  • Reconcile records and communicate the boundary — Configuration / change coordinator
Explore responsibilities and evidence →

Asset handover & acceptance

Transfer a defined asset and its support information to identified receiving responsibilities.

  • Define the receiving boundary — Asset recipient / responsible team
  • Assemble the relevant evidence — Configuration / change coordinator
  • Examine readiness from each receiving role — Asset recipient / responsible team

Separate the technology choices

Collection, electrical supply, propulsion and train control are distinct choices. Four selected arrangements compare third-rail DC, fourth-rail DC, overhead DC and overhead AC, including the normal return path and conversion equipment. The initial fictional arrangement pairs LIM propulsion with loop-based SelTrac control. Compare a rotary drive without changing the control medium, or loop and radio control without changing the motor. These are teaching examples, not assertions of commissioned combinations.

The LIM reaction rail is a passive electromagnetic secondary. The inductive cable is a communication medium. DC conductors supply traction energy. Operational voice and passenger communications can use radio even when train control uses a track loop.

Dedicated conventional-signalling, ETCS and supplier-generation studies show their named architectures. An ETCS level does not select an electrification supply or a motor type. Compare platform sensing and platform doors in the platform view.

Track & guideway

Running rail: head, web and foot

A shaped steel beam carries the wheel contact and passes its load into the track supports.

In a flat-bottom rail, the head provides the running surface, the web connects the section, and the broad foot meets the rail seat and restraints. Commercial profiles have different shapes and section properties.

The rail bridges adjacent supports. A wheel load therefore reaches several support points through bending, rather than dropping only into the sleeper directly beneath it. This is the load-path interpretation used in the model.

Wheel guidance also depends on the wheel and rail profiles together. The running rail is mechanically distinct from a traction conductor or a LIM reaction rail, even where they appear alongside it.

The section and wheel profiles are simplified; actual rail profiles are selected for the track and vehicles.

British Steel

Explore the equipment or system →
Ballasted track

Rails and sleepers sit in a granular support bed, forming a layered mechanical system.

Ballasted track combines running rails, their fastenings, sleepers and a bed of stone. The ballast supports the sleepers and helps preserve the track's geometry.

The model follows the load through this assembly: wheel to rail, rail seat to sleeper, then through the stone bed into the prepared foundation. Each layer has a different role; ballast is not a replacement for the fastening that holds the rail.

A cutaway makes the distinction visible: the rail is restrained locally at repeated seats, while the granular bed supports and surrounds the sleeper.

Layer depths, sleeper spacing and ballast shoulders vary with the track design.

Network Rail

Explore the equipment or system →
Ballast: support and drainage

The stone bed distributes load, restrains sleepers and provides connected spaces for drainage.

Ballast transfers sleeper loads through contacts between particles. Material around the sleeper also contributes lateral restraint, so the bed's function extends beyond vertical cushioning.

The spaces between particles provide drainage paths. Research on fouled ballast shows that fine material can fill these spaces, retain water and reduce the bed's ability to pass water.

Load transmission and drainage therefore use the same physical layer in different ways: forces travel through the particle contacts, while water travels through the connected voids. The model separates these two paths visually.

The animation compares water paths and particle contacts; it does not calculate drainage capacity.

Mid-America Transportation Center / University of Kansas

Explore the equipment or system →
Subballast and separation layer

An intermediate layer separates ballast from the foundation and spreads load.

Subballast sits between ballast and subgrade. Its functions include distributing load, limiting the mixing of adjacent materials and directing water toward drainage.

Its role differs from the open stone bed above. The model uses a finer layer and lateral drainage path to make that distinction visible.

Materials and drainage arrangements vary with ground conditions and track design.

Federal Railroad Administration / US Department of Transportation

Explore the equipment or system →
Formation and subgrade

The prepared foundation forms the largely hidden end of the track's load path.

The subgrade is the soil or other foundation material beneath the track layers. Its support and drainage behavior affect the structure built above it.

In this model, formation means the prepared upper foundation surface. A simplified soft-support animation demonstrates why sound rails alone cannot ensure stable geometry when their underlying support deforms.

Here, formation means the prepared upper foundation surface; terminology varies between railways.

Federal Railroad Administration / US Department of Transportation

Explore the equipment or system →
Sleeper or tie

A sleeper carries repeated rail seats, maintains their relationship and spreads forces into the support below.

Sleepers anchor the rails through their fastenings and transfer forces to the track substructure. Their geometry and materials are selected for the loading and environment.

The concrete sleeper shown here has two rail seats. These seats and their fastenings keep the rails in the intended lateral relationship while the sleeper distributes their loads over a larger supporting area.

An optional under-sleeper pad lies beneath the sleeper and changes its contact with ballast. It is a different component from the rail pad directly beneath a rail foot.

The example uses concrete sleepers. Timber, steel and composite sleepers are also used.

Vossloh

Explore the equipment or system →
Rail pad and resilient layer

An elastic layer between rail and support changes how wheel forces and vibration enter the track structure.

A rail pad sits beneath the rail foot at the support. In resilient fastenings, elastomeric pads allow controlled deflection and influence how vertical forces reach the supporting structure.

Changing the pad changes the support's force–deflection behavior. It can also change vibration transmission; the rail, fasteners and structure still act as a connected system.

The model exaggerates a small pad compression so its role becomes visible. It does not treat stiffness and damping as the same quantity or imply that the softest pad is automatically the best choice.

Pad stiffness and damping are different properties, both relevant to the track’s response.

Vossloh

Explore the equipment or system →
Elastic rail clip and shoulder

A spring element presses the rail into its seat while its anchor transfers restraint to the support.

An elastic rail fastening combines a spring clip with anchorage and contact components. The clip's elastic deflection produces a retaining force on the rail foot.

In the selected example, a shoulder anchors the clip, an insulator separates a contact interface, and a pad supports the rail. These components cooperate to restrain the rail while permitting the fastening's intended elastic movement.

The clip acts as a spring: its deflection presses the rail into its seat, while the shoulder transfers the reaction into the sleeper or baseplate.

Fastening families use different clip shapes, anchors and contact components.

Pandrol

Explore the equipment or system →
Rail-seat insulator

A small interface component can contribute both electrical separation and lateral positioning.

Rail fastenings can include insulating components at restraint interfaces. These separate conducting parts while transmitting mechanical contact forces.

Insulator geometry also matters mechanically: in some fastening families, changing the side component changes the rail's lateral position. The model shows that such a piece is part of the rail-seat geometry, not simply a colored electrical symbol.

One insulating piece does not establish whole-track insulation or define traction return.

Pandrol

Explore the equipment or system →
Baseplate and rail seat

A plate organizes the rail support, restraints and attachment to the structure beneath it.

A baseplate can carry the rail pad and fastening components on timber, composite or concrete supports. Different plate arrangements connect the same basic rail-seat functions to different foundations.

Some assemblies add resilience below the plate as well as below the rail. Separating those two levels explains why a fastening can have several layers without each layer being another rail pad.

Some fastenings add resilience below the plate as well as directly under the rail.

Pandrol

Explore the equipment or system →
Direct-fixation track

Individual rail supports attach to a structural base while retaining engineered resilience and restraint.

Direct fixation attaches rail-support assemblies to a slab or other structural support without an intervening ballast bed. The assembly can include a baseplate, anchors, resilient intermediate layers and electrical insulation.

The word direct describes the support arrangement. It does not mean that the rail must be rigidly fastened against bare concrete: the rail and plate can still deflect through their resilient layers.

In this model, wheel forces pass through the rail seat and fastening into the concrete support. The distinct mechanical and electrical interfaces remain visible in the cutaway.

Vossloh

Explore the equipment or system →
Slab track

A concrete structural layer supports the rail system in place of the conventional ballast bed.

Slab track is a family of constructions rather than one universal stack. One established approach combines precast rail-support blocks with a cast-in-place concrete track slab.

The structural slab and the rail support are different levels of the assembly. Concrete provides the supporting structure; the selected rail fastening supplies the local restraint and resilience.

The comparison model offers separate construction presets: embedded support blocks in a slab, or individual direct-fixation seats on concrete. Showing them separately avoids presenting components from different systems as one mandatory design.

RAILONE

Explore the equipment or system →
Concrete plinth

A raised concrete support places direct fasteners above the underlying slab or deck.

A plinth can take the form of a longitudinal concrete block supporting direct rail fasteners. It transfers forces into the underlying structure and establishes a support level above it.

The rail's final position follows the combined geometry of the structural support, plinth and fastening assembly. The plinth is therefore distinct from the small baseplate immediately below the rail seat.

In the section model, the plinth connects a close-up fastening assembly to the much larger guideway deck. This makes the change in structural scale visible without adopting a real installation's dimensions.

Eungcheol Kim, Myungseob Kim, Gabrielle Delos and Tyler Clark / Sustainability

Explore the equipment or system →
Embedded rail

A rail can receive continuous elastic support inside a channel rather than repeated exposed rail seats.

Embedded systems can surround the rail with resilient profiles or compounds that provide continuous vertical and lateral support. This differs from a rail held at widely separated sleeper seats.

The surrounding elastic system can also contribute vibration isolation and electrical separation. Embedded construction is therefore more than placing bare steel directly in concrete.

The street-context model removes a slice of paving to reveal the rail, resilient surround and supporting channel. The running surface and the wheel-flange path remain open; the exact exposed profile depends on the selected construction.

The street view illustrates rail support; it does not place exposed traction conductors in a street.

Turnout: one track to two routes

A turnout combines a movable switch, connecting rails and a crossing into one route-changing assembly.

The switch selects the entry path; closure rails connect that region to the crossing, or frog, where the rail paths intersect. These are distinct parts of the complete turnout.

The model follows a wheelset along either route. Route selection changes the switch geometry at the entry; it does not rotate every rail or move the fixed frog.

Explore the equipment or system →
Stock rail

The fixed rail provides the mating surface beside a movable switch rail.

At a switch, the stock rail and the tapered switch rail have coordinated contact geometry. Their relationship guides the wheel through the transition into the selected path.

The stock rail stays fixed while the closing switch blade approaches its mating face. Together they form the running edge for the selected route.

voestalpine Railway Systems · Bane NOR · Vossloh

Explore the equipment or system →
Switch rail or blade

A tapered movable rail changes which continuous wheel path is available through the switch.

A switch rail narrows toward its tip so its contact geometry can meet the stock rail and guide the wheel onto the chosen path.

The selected model uses flexible blades: one closes toward a stock rail as the other opens away. The animation emphasizes the changing contact relationship rather than treating the complete rail as a short rigid door hinge.

This example uses flexible switch blades; hinged designs also exist.

voestalpine Railway Systems · Bane NOR · Vossloh

Explore the equipment or system →
Closure rail

Connecting rails carry the running paths from the switch region toward the crossing.

Closure rails join the switch and frog within the turnout. They complete the connecting geometry between the route-selection region and the crossing.

These rails remain fixed while the switch blades move. Their curvature and alignment connect the selected path to the crossing.

voestalpine Railway Systems / Nortrak-Damy · Bane NOR · Vossloh

Explore the equipment or system →
Crossing or frog

A crossing lets one rail path pass through another while leaving space for wheel flanges.

A conventional fixed crossing includes a pointed vee, or nose, and wing rails around it. Flangeways provide passages through the intersecting rail geometry.

The wheel must pass from one supporting running surface to the next near this interruption. The model makes the nose, wing rails and flange passages visible instead of hiding them beneath a solid X-shaped block.

This is a fixed, tread-bearing example. Other crossing arrangements change the moving elements or the way the wheel is supported, so the same contact animation should not be applied to every frog type.

Some fixed frogs are self-guarded: raised parts of the frog casting guide the wheel at the crossing. These replace the separate check rails used in the conventional arrangement.

This example uses a fixed, tread-bearing crossing. Movable-nose and flange-bearing crossings work differently.

voestalpine Railway Systems · Bane NOR · Vossloh · voestalpine Railway Systems · RISSB

Explore the equipment or system →
Check rail or crossing guard rail

A guide beside the opposite running rail helps position the wheelset as the other wheel passes the frog.

A conventional crossing guard rail lies on the gauge side of the running rail opposite the frog. Its guiding action helps keep the wheelset aligned and protects the crossing nose.

The key relationship spans the axle: guiding one wheel helps position the wheel at the crossing on the other side. A single-wheel animation would hide this relationship.

The illustrated guide works against the inner back face of the wheel when contact is needed. It is not an extra normal tread-support rail, an electrical conductor or a LIM reaction rail.

Check-rail and guard-rail terminology varies. Derailment-containment rails elsewhere on the railway can serve a different purpose.

voestalpine Railway Systems Nortrak · Bane NOR · Vossloh

Explore the equipment or system →
Stretcher bar and blade linkage

A mechanical link coordinates the relationship between the two switch rails.

A stretcher bar connects switch rails so their positions remain related: one side can be closed while the other is open. The assembly includes the bar and its connecting parts.

Some arrangements include electrical insulation in the connection. That electrical separation does not remove the mechanical job of transmitting movement and maintaining the intended blade relationship.

In the model the linkage is distinct from a sleeper, which supports the rails, and from a detector, which reports their position. Linking, supporting and sensing are different functions.

Point machine and lock

A point-operating system moves the switch rails and provides the required locking function.

Point systems combine a drive with a locking arrangement; detection may be integrated or separate. Movement, retention and position reporting remain distinct functions.

The four-rod study gives each blade its own operating rod and detector rod. Two illustrated positive locks secure the operating slides. The exposed drive and lock layout is functional, rather than a reproduction of a supplier’s internal mechanism.

The cutaway combines published functions in a simplified four-rod arrangement.

Feedback reports the physical switch state rather than merely repeating the requested route.

The teaching model separates a requested route from confirmed position. A command or a stopped motor alone is not treated as proof that the blades and locking arrangement have reached the required state.

Crossover

Two connected turnouts allow a train to transfer between parallel tracks.

A crossover consists of a pair of turnouts joined between parallel tracks. The connection provides a route from one track to the other.

The model expands the single-turnout view to show both ends of that connecting route. A wheelset must follow compatible geometry through both turnouts, not merely cross a colored line between the tracks.

This differs from a diamond crossing: a plain diamond lets two alignments intersect but does not, by itself, provide a transfer between them.

Diamond crossing

Two tracks intersect at the same level while each continues along its own alignment.

A diamond places the rail intersections of two crossing tracks within one special-trackwork assembly. In a plain fixed diamond, the geometry does not select a transfer between the two alignments.

The wheel-support details matter at each intersection. Crossing products include different support arrangements, including flange-bearing alternatives, so there is no single contact animation that accurately describes every diamond.

The baseline model is a schematic fixed, tread-bearing example. It exposes the crossing gaps and guidance features while keeping the two through routes distinct.

A fixed diamond has two common crossings and two obtuse crossings. Its layout view marks these regions without animating a wheel-contact passage.

LIM reaction rail

The track-mounted secondary of the linear motor.

A short-primary arrangement puts the energized primary on the vehicle and the reaction plate along the track. The secondary is not the supply conductor.

In this model the reaction rail sits between the running rails. Its location and dimensions illustrate the coupling, without reproducing a railway design.

Track formation and earthwork

The formation is the prepared ground that supports the track layers.

Sleepers and ballast spread loads into the formation and earthwork below. Water can affect the strength and stability of that supporting ground.

Drainage and outfall

A culvert carries water through the ground beneath the railway.

The culvert needs a connected passage from its inlet to its outlet. Deposits, damage or a blocked outfall can affect that passage, including sections hidden from track level.

In Structures & drainage, inspect the sidewalls, invert (bottom slab) and crown (top slab) around the opening. The Infrastructure inspection & work evidence process connects a recorded condition with assessment, work and a follow-up check.

Bridge and support interfaces

A bridge transfers track loads through its deck and supports to the ground.

In this example, the deck passes load into girders, then through bearings into the abutments. Bearings support the deck while accommodating the movements allowed by their design.

Inspect the deck, bearings and abutments in Structures & drainage. A drainage repair and a bearing observation concern different parts of the asset and need their own evidence.

An inspection record identifies what was examined, where and what was found.

Culverts and other enclosed spaces can require inspection methods that reach beyond what is visible from track level. The record connects the observation to a specific asset and location.

In the maintenance process, begin with the observation and its assessment question. Keep evidence about the culvert separate from any observation about the nearby bridge.

A drainage repair has a defined scope and location. Coordinating that work also involves the people and arrangements that control access to the railway.

Repair and follow-up record

A work record says what was done; a follow-up check records what was found afterward.

Keep the original observation, completed work and follow-up evidence distinct. Each record needs an identifiable asset, location and date or version.

In the Infrastructure inspection & work evidence map, compare the actual end state with the review of evidence and continuing actions. A completed drainage check leaves a separate bridge issue open until that issue is addressed.

Two wheels connected by an axle follow the two running rails through the turnout.

In this tread-bearing example, the wheel tread carries vertical load on the rail head. The flange passes through the flangeway; its back face can provide lateral guidance against the check rail.

The wheelset follows the selected route. The picture shows where guidance and support occur; contact forces and vehicle dynamics require a separate calculation.

The pointed part of a common crossing carries the tread as support transfers from the wing rail.

The nose and its adjoining rails form the vee. The flange passage beside it allows the wheel on the intersecting route to pass.

This nose is fixed. A movable-nose crossing is a different arrangement with its own setting, locking and detection needs.

Traction transformer

A transformer transfers energy between separate winding circuits through a magnetic core.

The DC substation transformer supplies the rectifier. The conventional AC chain has a source-side traction transformer and a separate transformer on the train before the line converter.

Open the assembly to identify the core, primary and secondary windings, tank and insulated terminals. Follow each winding to its own electrical connections.

Siemens Mobility · Siemens Mobility · ABB · MIT OpenCourseWare

Explore the equipment or system →
Traction rectifier

The wayside diode rectifier supplies the DC traction network.

The rectifier changes the substation transformer’s AC output into DC. Its diode arrangement is one-way, so it cannot export regenerated energy to the AC grid. A receiving train or another available energy sink is needed on the DC side.

Open the assembly to inspect the clamped semiconductor devices, heat sinks, busbars and enclosure. The conventional AC supply chain omits this wayside rectifier.

The electrical-principle view follows an ideal six-diode bridge for one three-phase cycle. The phase at the highest voltage feeds the positive bus; the lowest phase provides the return. The DC output has six ripple pulses per input cycle.

DC switchgear

Distributes the DC output.

The rectifier supplies DC busbars, which distribute current through feeder circuits to track sections.

Circuit breakers protect the outgoing feeders and can disconnect a faulted circuit.

DC circuit breaker

Interrupts a protected circuit.

A protection device detects an abnormal electrical condition and initiates opening of the circuit breaker.

The breaker separates its contacts and extinguishes the arc to interrupt current. Direct current has no regular current-zero crossing, so a DC breaker needs an interruption design suited to that duty.

Siemens Mobility · Sécheron

Wayside braking resistor

Turns surplus electrical energy into heat.

During electrical braking, the train can deliver energy back to the DC network. If receptive loads are unavailable, suitably controlled resistors can absorb energy instead.

Resistors may be onboard or trackside. The enclosure and cooling path matter because the removed kinetic energy becomes heat; a resistor is not an energy store.

This example uses a trackside resistor; other railways use onboard resistors, energy storage or reversible substations.

Protective bonding and return

Distinguish traction return from protective bonding.

Return voltage and stray current need coordination. A voltage-limiting device is one available protection measure.

Earth is not the illustrated normal return. Bonding and return connections must not be treated as interchangeable paths.

Marks an isolation boundary.

A disconnector establishes an isolation gap in a circuit. This is a different function from interrupting fault current.

Some equipment combines isolation with load switching; the device type determines which currents it can interrupt.

Onboard traction transformer

The conventional AC train changes voltage through two separate winding circuits.

The pantograph supplies the primary winding. Magnetic coupling transfers energy to the secondary winding, which feeds the line converter.

The primary return runs through wheelsets and rails. Copper traces show the separate secondary circuit. This transformer appears only in the overhead AC example.

A DC link connects the supply conversion to the motor inverter.

In the conventional AC example, the transformer and line converter feed the DC link. The three DC examples feed the onboard DC circuit without those AC stages.

The motor inverter supplies the selected propulsion in every supply arrangement.

Rotary motors turn wheelsets through a mechanical drive. A linear induction motor (LIM) instead develops thrust by interacting with a reaction rail.

Changing between conductor rail and overhead collection keeps the propulsion choice. Follow the inverter output to see which motor receives the controlled electrical power.

The traction circuit needs a return connection to its source.

Fourth rail uses a separate return conductor and shoe in this model. Third rail, overhead DC and overhead AC use wheelsets and running rails as part of their return circuit.

Cyan traces identify the normal traction return. Protective earthing and bonding address electrical hazards; the two functions must be coordinated in the railway’s electrical design.

Transformer magnetic core

A magnetic core links the primary and secondary windings.

Alternating magnetic flux in the core transfers energy between the two winding circuits. The thin layers of a laminated core reduce losses caused by currents circulating within the core material.

Separate the core, winding groups, tank and terminals. Follow each winding to its own terminals: the shared magnetic path does not join the two electrical circuits.

Transformer primary winding

The primary winding receives the alternating supply.

An AC voltage across the primary establishes changing magnetic flux in the core. That flux induces a voltage in the secondary winding.

Amber identifies the primary winding groups. Compare them with the copper secondary groups and their separate terminals.

Transformer secondary winding

The secondary winding supplies the next electrical stage.

Magnetic coupling induces a voltage in this winding. In the DC substation it supplies the rectifier; on the conventional AC train it supplies the line converter.

Trace the secondary terminals to the downstream equipment. The separate winding circuit is electrically isolated from the primary in this two-winding transformer.

Vehicles & propulsion

Carbody and equipment zones

Houses people and the vehicle systems.

The body carries the passenger compartment and provides mounting space for vehicle equipment. The cutaway shows the passenger space, underframe equipment and roof services.

Suspension between the body and bogies carries the vehicle load while allowing relative movement as the train follows the track.

Bogie and wheelsets

Connect the carbody to the track.

The model groups the wheelsets, frame, suspension and friction-brake hardware so their mechanical relationships can be inspected together.

Bogie design influences vehicle dynamics and ride comfort. A LIM primary can provide thrust while the wheels continue to support and guide the vehicle.

Traction inverter / propulsion converter

Controls electrical power delivered to the motor.

A traction converter uses controlled power electronics to supply an AC motor. In the selected DC examples, it connects the conductor-rail supply to either the LIM primary or the rotary traction motors.

Its control, thermal management and protection work together. During electrical braking, compatible conversion equipment transfers generated energy back toward the DC supply.

Propulsion control unit (PCU) is a broader equipment label; the functions grouped inside it vary by manufacturer.

Siemens Mobility

Explore the equipment or system →
LIM primary

Produces the motor’s travelling magnetic field.

The train-mounted primary carries the energized windings. Magnetic coupling across the air gap induces current in the conducting secondary; their interaction produces longitudinal force.

Direct electromagnetic thrust does not require the wheels to transmit propulsion torque. In this illustrated wheel-supported train, the LIM is not a levitation system.

Railway Technical Research Institute · Massachusetts Institute of Technology — James L. Kirtley Jr.

Explore the equipment or system →
Travelling field, slip and air gap

Relative motion makes induction possible.

Slip is the relative speed between the travelling magnetic field and the secondary. That relative motion induces current in the secondary. At synchronous speed, the ideal induction model has zero slip.

Changing the field speed changes the direction and size of the interaction. Motoring and regenerative braking use different slip conditions. The air gap also affects magnetic coupling.

The animation illustrates magnetic interaction. A force calculation also needs motor geometry, material properties and operating conditions.

Massachusetts Institute of Technology — James L. Kirtley Jr.

Explore the equipment or system →
Blended braking and friction brakes

Several brake mechanisms cooperate to slow the train.

Brake control allocates the requested braking effort among available mechanisms. Electrical braking can recover energy; friction braking supplies additional or replacement effort when needed.

Wheel-slide protection monitors axle behaviour and adjusts braking effort when adhesion is limited. Braking performance depends on equipment, operating conditions and the selected control strategy.

Regenerative capability and brake blending vary across designs and operating conditions.

Knorr-Bremse

Explore the equipment or system →
Parking brake

Holds a stationary vehicle.

A parking brake holds a vehicle after it has stopped. Regenerative braking depends on motion and cannot provide this stationary holding function.

A spring-applied design uses stored spring force to apply the brake; another source of force releases it.

Knorr-Bremse

Explore the equipment or system →
Where braking energy goes

Energy needs a destination.

Electrical braking converts some motion into electrical energy. A receptive network can use it elsewhere; otherwise suitable resistors can dissipate it as heat. Available electrical braking depends on the equipment and the energy destination; friction braking is a separate part of the train's braking system.

Compare a receptive train with wayside resistor dissipation. The animation shows energy destinations, not a recovery percentage or stopping-distance prediction.

The selected diode rectifier cannot send energy backward into the AC utility. Grid regeneration needs suitable reversible equipment.

Supplies the train’s supporting electrical systems.

Auxiliary conversion provides suitable power for onboard applications separately from traction-motor conversion. A battery charger may be integrated with the auxiliary converter.

The scene connects this branch to comfort and service equipment to make the power split visible. Actual output voltages, redundancy and load allocations depend on the vehicle.

Which loads remain available after line power is lost, and for how long, depends on the vehicle’s battery capacity and distribution circuits.

Rotary traction motor

An electric motor develops torque that drives a wheelset in this selected arrangement.

The inverter supplies the motor with controlled electrical power. Its rotating electromagnetic field produces torque at a shaft; a coupling and gear unit transmit that torque to a driven axle. Wheel–rail adhesion then transfers the longitudinal force.

Compare this torque path with the LIM: the LIM primary exchanges electromagnetic force with a track-mounted reaction rail. The rotary example has a driven wheelset and does not need that LIM secondary. Either propulsion choice can be combined with a separately designed train-control system.

The example uses a geared rotary drive; direct-drive and other mechanical arrangements also exist.

Siemens Mobility · Siemens Mobility · Railway Technical Research Institute

Traction gearbox and axle drive

A gear unit couples rotary motor torque to the wheelset.

The motor usually turns faster than the driven axle. Reduction gears lower the output speed and increase axle torque, allowing the motor and wheels to operate at suitable speeds.

Torque passes through the gearbox to the wheelset, then through wheel–rail contact to move the train. The train-control system sends driving requests through a separate information path.

Siemens Mobility

Wheel–rail contact

Adhesion is the grip available where a wheel meets the rail.

Wheel torque becomes a driving or braking force through the contact with the rail. If the requested force exceeds the available grip, the wheel can spin during traction or slide during braking.

Compare the wheel’s rim marker with its moving centre. Spin means excess rotation for the distance travelled; slide means too little rotation. The rolling example provides the reference.

RSSB · Knorr-Bremse

Explore the equipment or system →
Applied traction and brake effort

A request for effort and the effort applied at the wheel are different quantities.

Traction and brake controls request effort. The equipment delivers torque at the wheel, while available wheel–rail grip limits the force that moves or slows the vehicle.

The bar represents applied effort: it changes with the brake actuator during wheel-slide protection. Compare that cue with wheel rotation and travel. LIM thrust acts through the reaction rail, outside this wheel-driven traction example.

RSSB · Knorr-Bremse

Explore the equipment or system →
Rotation and travel reference

Compare wheel rotation with the vehicle’s movement along the rail.

An axle sensor measures rotation. Wheel spin or slide can make a speed estimate based on that rotation differ from the vehicle’s actual speed.

The rim marker turns with the wheel. The separate travel marker follows its centre past the fixed stripes. These two visual cues help you see the difference between rotation and forward movement.

Wheel-slide protection adjusts applied braking effort to control wheel slide.

The controller monitors wheel behaviour and reduces or restores braking effort as needed. Reducing the brake torque can let a sliding wheel regain rotation.

In Slide protection, the actuator and effort bar change while the wheel turns. Sanding is a separate way to affect the grip available at the contact.

Train control

Automatic train protection · ATP

Supervises movement limits and can demand braking.

ATP checks whether train movement remains inside its permitted envelope. ETCS provides one public example: onboard supervision compares position and speed with applicable limits, predicts the approach to a target, and can command brake intervention.

The protection computer issues a braking command; the vehicle braking equipment produces the physical force. An ATO driving request remains within the limits supervised by ATP.

Specific supervision functions, margins and intervention rules depend on the system.

European Union Agency for Railways

Explore the equipment or system →
Automatic train operation · ATO

Drives toward operational targets within protection constraints.

ATO calculates driving actions such as acceleration, coasting and braking from the journey target and the information available to it. In the published ATO-over-ETCS arrangement, timetable information arrives from an ATO trackside function, while onboard ATO interfaces with traction and brakes.

ETCS retains the protection responsibility and determines when ATO may operate. Automation grade also describes who performs tasks: automatic driving can coexist with a driver in the cab. Driverless operation brings additional operational and supervision requirements; selecting ATO alone does not establish them.

The example explains ATO over ETCS; metro implementations allocate interfaces differently.

ERTMS Users Group

Explore the equipment or system →
Automatic train supervision · ATS

Coordinates the service across a line or network.

ATS gives controllers a network view and supports traffic regulation, timetable recovery, incident handling and service changes. A regulation decision might hold a train, adjust a departure or request a different service pattern. These are operating objectives that still pass through the applicable route and protection functions.

A control centre can also display traction-power SCADA, communications and security systems. Integration in one room or screen does not make those functions identical. Alstom publishes separate modules for these responsibilities, alongside its traffic-supervision and regulation tools.

Control-centre architecture and the scope of ATS vary by project.

Alstom

Explore the equipment or system →
Onboard train-control computer

Connects train information, protection and driving functions.

An onboard control function reports train position and receives information governing movement. Mitsubishi Electric describes an arrangement exchanging these messages with a wayside zone controller, enabling automatic driving within the applicable speed restriction.

Localization estimates where the train is, protection supervises its movement limits, and driving control requests traction or braking. The lines between these functions carry commands and feedback; motor power follows a separate electrical path.

Functional boxes do not specify the number of computers or their physical allocation.

Mitsubishi Electric

Train control and management system · TCMS

Coordinates vehicle equipment and reports its condition.

A TCMS connects commands, status and diagnostics across subsystems such as traction, braking, doors, lighting and HVAC.

A driving request travels to the propulsion controller, and equipment status returns to the TCMS. Vehicle management and movement permission have different responsibilities, even when their computers are integrated.

Hardware integration and the TCMS boundary are supplier- and project-dependent.

Wayside zone controller

Uses train reports to support control within an area.

In the example architecture, the zone controller receives train position reports and returns movement-related control information. The published Mitsubishi Electric arrangement addresses separation, speed and route control through exchanges between onboard and wayside equipment.

The model shows a report arriving before a response is delivered. A message contains information, not traction energy. Cabinet location, controller boundaries and the division of functions are implementation choices.

A zone-controller box is one architecture, not a universal CBTC requirement.

Explore the equipment or system →
Balise and onboard reader

Transfers localized track information as the train passes.

A Eurobalise is a track-mounted transponder energized by a passing train’s reader antenna. It provides a data telegram containing fixed or switchable information, such as a location reference or infrastructure data. The onboard balise transmission module processes the received message.

The train moves beyond the brief contact region and continues onboard supervision. A balise therefore is not a continuous radio access point, a wheel counter or a traction power source.

Eurobalise is the ETCS example; metro transponder functions and formats differ.

European Commission, Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport

Explore the equipment or system →
Wheel-speed sensor · tachometer

Measures wheel rotation for motion estimation.

Wheel rotation estimates speed and distance using a wheel-size assumption.

A sliding wheel can misrepresent vehicle speed. Compare its estimate with independent information.

This wheel-supported LIM example demonstrates friction-braking wheel slide; propulsion force is developed by the linear motor.

German Aerospace Center (DLR), Oliver Heirich and Benjamin Siebler

Explore the equipment or system →
Accelerometer and inertial measurement unit

Add an independent view of vehicle motion.

Acceleration and rotational measurements complement wheel-based odometry.

Integration accumulates error. Combining complementary measurements and position references can constrain drift; localization still retains uncertainty.

Sensor selection and estimation algorithms vary.

Deutsche Bahn — Digitale Schiene Deutschland · German Aerospace Center (DLR), Oliver Heirich and Benjamin Siebler

Explore the equipment or system →
Brake controller and wheel-slide protection

Translate braking demand into coordinated braking action.

Brake control coordinates available brake systems and can account for vehicle load. Wheel-slide protection is one of its supporting functions.

A braking command and the resulting deceleration are different quantities. Sensors provide feedback; a command alone is not proof that the train has slowed.

Brake blending, assurance and emergency arrangements are system-specific.

Knorr-Bremse
